title: Trigonometry
summary: Ratios, the standard-value table, the three identities, complementary angles, value-putting and max-min values. Tier 1 reliably holds 2-4 trig questions and they fall almost mechanically to the value table, one identity, or a 3-4-5 style triangle — among the cheapest marks in the paper.

subtopics.title: Ratios and standard values
subtopics.concept:
For an acute angle $\theta$ in a right triangle: $\sin\theta=\frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$,
$\cos\theta=\frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$, and
$\text{cosec}=\frac1{\sin}$, $\sec=\frac1{\cos}$, $\cot=\frac1{\tan}$.

**Standard value table (memorise cold — most CGL questions are one lookup away):**

| $\theta$ | $0^\circ$ | $30^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $90^\circ$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin$ | $0$ | $\frac12$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $\cos$ | $1$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | $\frac12$ | $0$ |
| $\tan$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3$ | undef. |

tricks.title: The 1-2-3 memory trick for sin
tricks.body:
Write $\frac{\sqrt0}{2},\frac{\sqrt1}{2},\frac{\sqrt2}{2},\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac{\sqrt4}{2}$ for
$0^\circ,30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ,90^\circ$ — the sin row falls out; the cos row is the same read backwards.
Divide the two rows to get tan.

tricks.title: Reciprocal first, table second
tricks.body: When an expression has cosec/sec/cot, flip each to sin/cos/tan before touching the table.

mistakes: $\tan90^\circ$ treated as $0$ or $1$ — it is undefined.
Reciprocal flipped the wrong way ($\sec\theta$ taken as $\frac{1}{\sin\theta}$).

subtopics.title: Fundamental identities
subtopics.concept:
Three identities drive almost every simplification:
$$\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1,\qquad 1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta,\qquad 1+\cot^2\theta=\text{cosec}^2\theta$$
Each splits into handy parts: $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$, $\sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta=1$,
$\text{cosec}^2\theta-\cot^2\theta=1$. Expressions with $\sin^6+\cos^6$ or $\sin^4+\cos^4$ reduce through
these — treat $x=\sin^2\theta$ so $x+(1-x)=1$.

tricks.title: Substitute $x=\sin^2\theta$
tricks.body: Everything above degree 4 collapses with $x$ and $1-x$. Memorise the two reduced forms for 4th and 6th powers.

tricks.title: Sec/tan pairs move as one
tricks.body:
See $\sec^2$ and $\tan^2$ together → replace by 1 (or by each other via $\sec^2=1+\tan^2$). Same for
cosec/cot.

mistakes: Expanding $\sin^6+\cos^6$ as $(\sin^2+\cos^2)^3$ without subtracting the cross terms.

subtopics.title: Complementary angles
subtopics.concept:
For angles that add to $90^\circ$:
$$\sin(90^\circ-\theta)=\cos\theta,\quad \tan(90^\circ-\theta)=\cot\theta,\quad \sec(90^\circ-\theta)=\text{cosec}\theta$$
and similarly in reverse. This converts "odd" angles ($67\tfrac12^\circ$, $72^\circ$, ...) into their partners and
makes paired products equal 1: $\tan\theta\cdot\tan(90^\circ-\theta)=1$.

An equation like $\sin(A+\theta)=\cos(B+\theta)$ forces $(A+\theta)+(B+\theta)=90^\circ$.

tricks.title: Pair the angles that add to 90°
tricks.body:
In a long product, look for $\theta$ and $90-\theta$ pairs first — each pair collapses to 1. The classic
$\tan1^\circ\tan2^\circ\cdots\tan89^\circ$ collapses completely.

tricks.title: Convert everything to one angle
tricks.body:
Rewrite each term at its complementary partner until only one angle remains; a $\sin^2+\cos^2$ pair may then
collapse.

tricks.title: Equation → sum to 90°
tricks.body: When $\sin(\ldots)=\cos(\ldots)$, set the two bracketed angles to sum to $90^\circ$ and solve.

example.q: If $\sin(40^\circ+\theta)=\cos(30^\circ+\theta)$ and both angles are acute, find $\theta$.

mistakes: Complementary conversion applied to the wrong function ($\sec(90-\theta)=\sec\theta$ is wrong).
Setting $\sin A=\cos B\Rightarrow A+B=180^\circ$ — it is $90^\circ$.
Products paired as $\tan\theta\cdot\cot\theta=1$ but evaluated before converting to the same angle.

subtopics.title: Value-putting and given-ratio questions
subtopics.concept:
Two CGL workhorses:

1. **Given one ratio, draw the triangle.** If $\sin\theta=\frac{5}{13}$, take opposite $=5$, hypotenuse $=13$,
   adjacent $=\sqrt{13^2-5^2}=12$ (a 5-12-13 triplet!) and read off every other ratio.
2. **Value-putting an identity.** If only $\sin\theta+\text{cosec}\theta$ or a quadratic condition like
   $\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$ is given, convert the asked expression into the given pieces — or test a
   convenient $\theta$ when the expression is identically constant.

formulas.name: Sum-product of a ratio and reciprocal

tricks.title: Draw the triplet triangle
tricks.body: Ratio given → sides in hand in 5 seconds. Check the triplet table before any algebra.

tricks.title: Reduce the asked expression
tricks.body: Rewrite the target in terms of the given relation. For $x+\frac1x$ chains, square and subtract 2.

mistakes: Triplets applied with hypotenuse as a leg ($\sqrt{13^2-12^2}$ vs $\sqrt{13^2+12^2}$).
Forgetting that a given ratio fixes $	heta$ up to the quadrant — CGL keeps $	heta$ acute, so take the positive root.
Value-putting with $\theta=45^\circ$ when the expression is not constant — verify a second angle before trusting it.

subtopics.title: Maximum and minimum values
subtopics.concept:
For $0^\circ\le\theta\le90^\circ$:
- $0\le\sin\theta,\cos\theta\le1$; $\sec\theta,\text{cosec}\theta\ge1$; $\tan\theta,\cot\theta$ are unbounded.
- $\sin\theta+\cos\theta\in[1,\sqrt2]$; $\sin\theta-\cos\theta\in[-1,1]$; $\sin\theta\cos\theta\le\frac12$.
- $a\sin^2\theta+b\cos^2\theta$ has minimum $\min(a,b)$ and maximum $\max(a,b)$.
- $a\tan^2\theta+b\cot^2\theta\ (\text{and } a\sin^2+b\,\text{cosec}^2)$ has minimum $2\sqrt{ab}$ by AM–GM.
- $\sec^2\theta+\text{cosec}^2\theta$ has minimum $2+2=4$ (at $45^\circ$).

tricks.title: Match the question to a range
tricks.body: Bounded pairs ($\sin+\cos$ etc.) → memorised range. Weighted square sums → min of coefficients or $2\sqrt{ab}$.

example.q: Find the minimum value of $4\tan^2\theta+9\cot^2\theta$ for $0^\circ<\theta<90^\circ$.

tricks.title: Weighted sin-cos squares are bounded by coefficients
tricks.body: $2\sin^2\theta+3\cos^2\theta=2+\cos^2\theta$, so it ranges from 2 to 3 — min 2, max 3, no calculus.

mistakes: AM-GM applied to $a\sin\theta+b\text{cosec}\theta$ where the equality point may be unreachable — for the square versions it is safe, check before using.
Quoting $\sqrt2$ as the **minimum** of $\sin+\cos$ — $\sqrt2$ is the maximum.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A short expression built from $0^\circ,30^\circ,45^\circ,60^\circ,90^\circ$ values.
pyqPatterns.approach: Flip reciprocals first, then read the table; the answer is usually 0, 1 or 2 — use it to sanity-check.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: $\sin\theta=\frac{p}{h}$ (or tan/cos) given; find another ratio or an expression in two of them.
pyqPatterns.approach: Triplet triangle: adjacent $=\sqrt{h^2-p^2}$; read all ratios at once.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Angles like $70^\circ$ beside $20^\circ$, or $\sin(90-\theta)$ inside expressions, or long tan products.
pyqPatterns.approach: Pair angles summing to $90^\circ$ (each product = 1); convert to one function family; equation form gives $A+B+2\theta=90^\circ$.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Expressions in $\sin^4+\cos^4$, $\sin^6+\cos^6$, $\sec^2-\tan^2$ chains; answer often constant.

pyqPatterns.approach: Bounded → coefficient min/max; unbounded reciprocal pairs → $2\sqrt{ab}$.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A condition like $\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$ or $\text{cosec}\theta+\cot\theta=k$; find a related expression.

solvedExamples.shortcut: Recognise the form: $\frac{2t}{1-t^2}=\tan2\theta$ with $\theta=30^\circ$ → $\tan60^\circ=\sqrt3$, no fractions at all.

solvedExamples.q: If $\cos\theta=\dfrac{7}{25}$, then the value of $\tan\theta$ is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: 7-24-25 triplet: see 7 and 25, write 24 instantly. Trap: $\frac{7}{24}$ is $\cot\theta$.

solvedExamples.solution:
Pair $\tan\theta$ with $\tan(90^\circ-\theta)=\cot\theta$: each pair multiplies to 1.

44 such pairs plus $\tan45^\circ=1$ give the product 1.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Every angle pairs with its complement; middle term is $\tan45^\circ=1$. Product $=1$.
Reduce each bracket to a single fraction; the $\sin^2\cos^2$ cancels completely → 1. (Check at $45^\circ$: $(\frac{1}{\sqrt2})^2\times2=1$.)

solvedExamples.solution:
$a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta$ peaks at $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$: here $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ (at $\tan\theta=\frac34$).

So the greatest value of the expression is $5+5=10$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=5$ for the trig part, then add the constant: $5+5=10$. Trap: 12 (added $3+4+5$ directly).
solvedExamples.pattern: max of a sin + b cos + c

practice.shortcut: This is $\sin(60+30)=\sin90^\circ=1$ — recognise the sine-addition shape instead of multiplying.
Divide through by $\cos\theta$: $(t+1)/(t-1)$ with $t=\frac34$ → $-7$. (Same trick works for any sin/cos ratio expression.)
practice.pattern: divide by cos to use tan

practice.q: If $\sin(40^\circ+\theta)=\cos(30^\circ+\theta)$, where both angles are acute, then $\theta$ equals:
practice.pattern: sin A = cos B angle equation

practice.q: If $\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$, then the value of $\cos^2\theta+\cos^4\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
From the condition, $\sin^2\theta=1-\sin\theta$, so $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta=\sin\theta$.

Then $\cos^4\theta=\sin^2\theta=1-\sin\theta$.

Sum $=\sin\theta+1-\sin\theta=1$.

practice.q: The minimum value of $\sin\theta+\cos\theta$ for $0^\circ\le\theta\le90^\circ$ is:
practice.solution: $\sin\theta+\cos\theta$ ranges from 1 (at $\theta=0^\circ$ or $90^\circ$) to $\sqrt2$ (at $45^\circ$). The minimum is 1.
practice.shortcut: Range $[1,\sqrt2]$: min 1, max $\sqrt2$. Trap: $\sqrt2$ is the **maximum**.
The $s^2c^2$ terms cancel exactly: $-6+6=0$ → answer 0 for every $\theta$. (Try $\theta=45^\circ$ to confirm.)

practice.q: The minimum value of $4\tan^2\theta+9\cot^2\theta$ (for acute $\theta$) is:
practice.solution:
By AM–GM, $4\tan^2\theta+9\cot^2\theta\ge2\sqrt{4\times9}=12$,

with equality when $2\tan\theta=3\cot\theta$, i.e. $\tan^2\theta=\frac32$ (reachable since tan is unbounded).

practice.shortcut: Companion is $\frac1k=\frac13$; average the pair: cosec $=\frac{3+\frac13}{2}=\frac53$ → $\sin=\frac35$.

practice.solution:
Write the brackets as $[t+(s-1)][t-(s-1)]=t^2-(s-1)^2$ where $t=\tan\theta$, $s=\sec\theta$.

$=t^2-s^2+2s-1=-1+2s-1=2(\sec\theta-1)$, using $s^2-t^2=1$.
practice.shortcut: Difference of squares, then $t^2-s^2=-1$: answer $2(\sec\theta-1)$. Quick check at $30^\circ$: LHS $\approx0.309$ = RHS.

practice.solution:
Write the left side as $2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)+5\cos^2\theta=2+5\cos^2\theta$.

So $2+5\cos^2\theta=6\Rightarrow\cos^2\theta=\frac45$, hence $\sin^2\theta=\frac15$.

$\tan^2\theta=\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}=\frac{1/5}{4/5}=\frac14\Rightarrow\tan\theta=\frac12$ (acute).
practice.shortcut: Anchor to $a(\sin^2+\cos^2)+(b-a)\cos^2$: solve for $\cos^2$, then $\tan^2=\frac{1-\cos^2}{\cos^2}$. Traps: 2 (reciprocal), $\frac14$ ($\tan^2$, forgot the root).
